messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Raúl Mendez was 62, a single psychiatrist who had spent most of his adult life in the United States after leaving a Latin American country that, in his telling, had once felt like an extension of himself. Decades later, he still dressed carefully for work, kept his office orderly, and spoke with the measured confidence of someone used to listening to other people’s pain. What he did not say easily was how a political detention in his twenties had turned his own body into a record of torture. He had been taken by men in uniform, held in an interrogation room where voices overlapped in rapid, incomprehensible chatter, and beaten and shocked until time fractured. He remembered flashes with unbearable clarity — the metal chair, the smell of sweat and disinfectant, a gloved hand, a boot, the sound of his own breathing — while other stretches were simply gone, as if someone had cut pages out of his life. When the memory returned, it did not feel distant or narrated; it came back fully, across all his senses at once, and for a moment he was there again, convinced that the room, the pain, and the terror were happening now.

The old experience stayed raw because reminders could arrive from almost anywhere. A news segment about unrest in a Latin American capital, a passing clip of detainees being led away, or the sight of officers in uniform at a courthouse could make him go cold in an instant. So could the sound of multiple people talking over one another in a way he could not parse, especially when it came from a television in a waiting room or a crowded hospital corridor. In those moments the memory seemed to seize him without warning, as if some detail in the world had opened a trapdoor. What frightened Raúl most was that each reminder seemed to confirm what he had come to believe: that the people and institutions that should have protected him had failed him, that no one had ever been held accountable, and that he had lost his connection to the community and culture that once gave his life meaning. The news did not merely remind him of the past; it seemed to tell him again that the same kind of power could still act with impunity, and that what had happened to him had been allowed to happen.

When the memory surged, Raúl’s mind raced back over those accusations. He would relive the torture with such vividness that his body reacted before his thoughts could catch up, and afterward he would hear himself making the same grim conclusions: that the institutions meant to protect him had abandoned him, that the men responsible had faced no consequences, and that something in him had been severed from his language, his people, and the country he once belonged to. The more complete the reliving felt, the more absolute those beliefs became. He started to dread even ordinary encounters because they could set off the same cascade. A uniform at the entrance to his building, a police officer near the subway, a flurry of unintelligible chatter in the lobby of his clinic, or a news alert on his phone could all bring the whole thing back. To keep that from happening, he began avoiding going out whenever he could. He arranged deliveries, declined invitations, and reduced errands to the minimum. At work, he rehearsed what he would say before almost any interaction, silently scripting greetings and questions so he would not be caught off guard by a stray phrase or a confusing exchange. If the sensation of the memory started to rise, he tried to redirect himself and think of something else, forcing his attention onto chart notes or mundane tasks.

Those efforts brought only brief relief. Rehearsing conversations and mentally steering away from the torture kept him tense and hyperfocused on what might go wrong, which made him even more alert to uniforms, voices, and news reports. Because he was always scanning for the next reminder, he noticed the wrong thing more often: a television in the pharmacy showing footage of a protest, a security guard in a dark jacket, two assistants talking too quickly in Spanish with an unfamiliar accent. Each avoidance practice also seemed to feed the memory rather than quiet it, because every time he escaped an outing or fixed his words in advance, he felt newly certain that the world outside his routines was unsafe and that his life had narrowed around what had been done to him. The more he withdrew, the more disconnected he felt from his community and culture, and the more the old belief hardened that no one had ever answered for the abuse. Even in his own profession, he found himself using work as a buffer, staying behind the office door and keeping relationships formal.

By the time he sought help, Raúl was exhausted by the shrinking of his world. He could still function on the surface, but the effort of containing the memories, the dread of news and uniforms, and the constant need to manage every interaction had become unbearable. What finally brought him in was a recent morning in the clinic when a loud, overlapping conversation from the hallway and a news alert about detentions abroad collided with the smell of disinfectant, and for a few seconds he was back in the room again, certain he could feel the chair and hear the men. He now feared that if this pattern kept tightening, he would withdraw completely; he hoped, more quietly, that treatment might help him reclaim some sense of safety, connection, and place in the world that had been taken from him.
